t: Cao Cao's southern campaign, begun in the autumn of 208, brought him Jiangling and a large fleet before it was halted on the Yangtze.
The allies fought on the river, and a feigned surrender by Huang Gai set Cao Cao's chained ships ablaze.
The battle fixed the Yangtze as a frontier, the basis of the later states of Shu Han and Eastern Wu, though its exact site is still disputed.
dyk: Cao Cao wrote to Sun Quan claiming an army of 800,000, while Zhou Yu put his strength nearer 230,000, including between 70 and 80 thousand men impressed from Ying.
ev: Cao Cao defeats his main rival Yuan Shao at Guandu and gains control of the North China Plain
Cao Cao defeats the Wuhuan at White Wolf Mountain, securing his northern flank
Cao Cao's southern campaign begins in the autumn; Liu Cong surrenders Jiangling and a sizeable fleet to him
Liu Bei is defeated at Changban and retreats east; Zhuge Liang negotiates an alliance with Sun Quan
The allied fleet meets Cao Cao's vanguard at Red Cliffs, and Huang Gai's fire ships set Cao Cao's fleet ablaze
Cao Cao retreats along Huarong Road; Jiangling falls to Zhou Yu by the end of the year
Zhou Yu dies, weakening Sun Quan's position in Jing Province
The Three Kingdoms period begins, with Shu Han and Eastern Wu resting on the frontiers fixed at Red Cliffs

f.date: Winter of 208–209 CE; historians differ on the timeline of events
f.place: On the Yangtze River in Jing Province, China; the exact site is disputed, with candidates southwest of present-day Wuhan and near Chibi City in Hubei
f.sides: The allies Sun Quan (commander Zhou Yu), Liu Bei and Liu Qi, about 50,000 marines in all, against Cao Cao, who claimed 800,000 men while Zhou Yu estimated about 230,000
f.outcome: The allies drove Cao Cao's fleet and army back; Cao Cao escaped north and never again commanded so large a fleet, while Liu Bei and Sun Quan kept the lands south of the Yangtze.
